title: Ang 1254–1256: Malar begins
hookLine: Guru Nanak opens the monsoon raga
tomorrow: Bebe misses Simran already. how, when she hasn't even left?

lines: THE AIR GOES HEAVY AND GREEN.
cards: Late afternoon at the truck yard, and the air goes strange: heavy, a little green. The smell arrives before the rain does, hot asphalt and dust going dark in spots. Drivers climb down from their cabs.
Harjit, who never stops working, stands in the open bay door with his hands in his pockets, just breathing it in. Simran films the first fat drops on the windshields, then puts the phone away.
The Granth has a whole raga made for this.

teach.h: MALAR: THE RAGA OF THE RAINS.
teach.b: It's called Malar, and it begins on ang 1254 with Guru Nanak.

Tradition ties Malar to the monsoon, the season when the clouds finally break after the long heat, and its hymns are full of that weather: dark clouds, thunder, the peacock, a small bird that cries for a single drop.

teach.h: NOT TO MAKE RAIN, BUT A PICTURE.
teach.b: A popular story says singing Malar can make it rain. The Granth's hymns aren't trying to. They use the rain as a picture.
Here's something to tell a friend tonight: Guru Nanak's first hymn in the raga of the rains doesn't open on clouds at all.
In paraphrase, it opens on ordinary days, eating, drinking, laughing, sleeping, and how easily they let us forget that life is short. The storm comes in through that door.

teach.h: THE DRY FIELD, AND THE CLOUD.
teach.b: In these hymns the body is the dry field, and the Name is the cloud.
When the rain comes, the drought inside breaks too. Notice how the raga works on the senses before the mind. You can hear the weather gathering in the music before a single word explains it.
Back at the yard, the rain stops as fast as it started. The asphalt steams. Harjit goes back to his desk without saying anything, but he leaves the bay door open.

how: Ragis sing the Malar hymns in kirtan, especially in the rainy season; readers find Guru Nanak's hymns at the start of the raga under the heading Mahala 1.

games.q: the raga of the rains — tap the pairs.

s: in the Granth, Malar is sung in order to make it rain
a popular story says so; the hymns use rain as a picture of what a dry life waits for.
Guru Nanak's first hymn in Malar opens with clouds and thunder
it opens on ordinary days, eating, drinking, laughing, sleeping, and how they help us forget.
in the Malar hymns, rain is a picture of the Name reaching a dry life
the body is the field, the Name is the cloud.

games.q: a long dry stretch: weeks of busy, ordinary days and nothing that feeds you. with Malar's first hymn in mind, what's the first step?
o: notice what the ordinary days have let you forget.
wait; the rain will come on its own schedule.
fill the days fuller so there's no time to feel dry.
games.why: Guru Nanak's first Malar hymn opens on eating, drinking, laughing, sleeping, and the forgetting they bring. noticing the drought comes before the rain.

practice: If you can, pour a little water into a glass, slowly, and listen to it fill. Take one sip and hold it in your mouth a moment before you swallow, the way dry ground holds the first rain.
Then sit and listen for any water sound that's left, or just your breath. If you'd like, read ang 1254 before you begin.
